utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I left Pirici on the 22nd of March, 1993. That is when I left the municipality of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Before you left Pirici, municipality of Vitez, did you have to ask for permission?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of a passport did you have at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Still the same one, the old one, the Yugoslavia Slav, the former one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the Croatian passport too?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when you left Vitez, did you have to seek permission from someone?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We needed permission to go through Croatia, I mean, a pass through Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you ask it from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the municipality to ask them to allow me to go there and bring my family home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Was it easy to get that certificate or did you have to ask, to beg, kneel down, or what, or did you simply apply for it and they give you the permission so that you could get out of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What means of transportation did you use?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I had an official car to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Zagreb I waited for the visa, because I needed a visa to cross over.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At the German embassy in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you get it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I waited for three days. I went back to my brother, in Rijeka, in Croatia, and I spend two days with him, then I went to Germany. I did not get a visa but I started to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And how was it at the Austrian and German border?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I crossed, illegally, the boarder because I didn't get --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, didn't you try to cross it lawfully?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to cross with a passport and I was given Zuruck.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So why?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because I did not have the visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So how did you cross the border?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I crossed on a bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So when you crossed into Germany for the second time, when was that? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I crossed over it was the 1st of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And from the 1st of April, 1993 until when did you not come back to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Until '95, June '95.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Is that when you came back?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Alone or with your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: First I came alone because in my sister was getting married in June. Twenty days later I went back to Germany and then came back home with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you entered Germany illegally, so when you were already in Germany, did you try to go somewhere legal to make your stay in Germany legal?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you support yourself or what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My wife worked and I also worked, even if illegally, so that we both worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were leaving Germany, what papers did you have to get out?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had the passport, because my brother sent me from Umag the passport to Germany, and he sent it to me through a colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you now had a Croatian passport.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I then had a Croatia passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, when you went to fetch your family, why didn't you then come back with your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you went to Germany for the second time to bring your family, or to visit your family. Never mind. Then how is it that you did not return to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I arrived late, two days, so that I could stay longer, until the 16th or 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So why didn't you come back?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My brother called me. I don't exactly remember the date. When he started, he told -- I said we should pack, and he told us, "Don't do that, because there is a war over here."

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That is the brother in Vitez who let you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the brother in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But when you returned to Vitez once and for all, did you suffer any consequences for having stayed abroad?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please then repeat just when did your mother-in-law, that is your wife's mother, when did she go to Germany for work?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, she's worked there are for 20 or 25 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You wouldn't know the dates; would you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when did she retire?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She retired in 1990 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: -- 94, I think. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did she come back to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, she didn't back to Vitez. She went to Croatia, near Osejak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when did she come to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it must be a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, during the first conflict, you were in Vitez then. Do you know whose house your sister and mother sought shelter in?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In my brother Rudo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Rudo what?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Rudo Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleague, Par, will ask questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I will ask a few more questions related to your departure to Germany and your stay in Germany. You answered that you left Pirici on the 22nd of March, 1993 to go to Germany, and that on that occasion the HVO gave you a permit to travel. Now I will show you a document and ask you if it is that certificate, if it is that permit which was issued to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you please, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D28/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you please have a look at this document and just tell us, for the record, who is the subject, what are the dates, and the purpose, the destination, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a permit to Mr. Mirko Vidovic, from the 22nd of March, 1993 until the 11th of April, 1993, to travel to Germany, transit through Croatia -- Republic of Croatia for the purpose of taking his family home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I should also like to ask you: Can you see here the boarder permit of the Republic of Croatia, that is, can we see the date when you entered the Republic of Croatia on the basis of this permit?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. 22nd of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And that is the border crossing?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Kamensko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, I want to have a look at your passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you be so kind?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D29/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you please look at it and tell us if this is the photocopy of the passport that you used at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the former Yugoslav passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you please turn to page 2 where there are all these stamps, to see if we can see that Zuruck from Germany, as you called it, that stamp. Page 2?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: There is no date, but do you see there written Deutschland Bundesrepublik? Do you see it says that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But down there you have Zuruck visa, so is that the stamp that you returned across the boarder?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do but I can't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: There is no date. All right. Thank you. So this is all. We do not need the passport now. You said you stayed in Germany illegally while you were away with your family. Did you ask for any papers from the City of the Frankfurt am Main at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what kind of a document you applied for and what form?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I applied for -- I said I had lost my passport and that I wanted to go to Croatia. Then they gave me a paper so that I could get out of Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, I would again like to ask you to show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D30/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, is that the document that you applied for from the city of Frankfurt?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Please, on this document, we can see some dates. First, the 29th of July, '93. Could you tell us, what is this date?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this date means the day they applied to the police for this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: To get out of the country?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: And the 6th of August, '93?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: 6th of August means that I was to leave Germany on the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Does it mean, on the basis of this paper, you were allowed to stay in Frankfurt until the 6th of August, and you say you stayed the there until June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because I did not have a document to cross, I spoke to my brother, and he said "Well, you can get out of Germany, but you cannot enter Slovenia with this paper."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: But you left with a Croatian passport, with a completely different document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I left with a Croatian passport, but he submitted documents in Umag, and he said, "You have to wait until we get your passport ready for you."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So in June '95, you say you came to attend your sister's wedding. What is your sister's name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Gordana Vidovic. And now she is married, Cuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: On the basis of what you said so far, you said that on the 22nd of March, '93, until June '95, you were in Germany. Does that mean that you spent in Germany all that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: That is, from the 21st of April, when you entered Germany, until June '95?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, a witness here said that on the 15th of April -- that is, on the eve of the Ahmici conflicts, he saw you sitting in the company of Vlatko Kupreskic and several soldiers in front of the Sutra store in Pirici. Could you tell us if that is true?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vidovic. My name is Franck Terrier. I'm one of the prosecutors representing the Office of the Prosecutor, and I'm going to ask a couple of questions of you if I may do so. First of all, Mr. Vidovic, can you tell us where you presently live?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Vitez, in the village of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you mean the house which you showed earlier on in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Together with your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your occupation, your professional occupation was in 1992 and '93?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was a salesman in a shop until the 21st of March, '93 -- 22nd -- no, the 21st, because on the 22nd I left for Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, Mr. Vidovic, as to this trade. What kind of trade was it, in what kind of field? Who were your business partners?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My business partners were Muslims, there were also Serbs, and we worked together. It was a hardware store. We dealt in building materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And where was that shop or that company, Mr. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And were you the owner of that shop in building materials?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us dwell for a moment on the village guards in which you took part, as you stated, especially so in 1992. Still, I would like to know whether at the time, in Pirici, Santici, Ahmici, whether there wasn't after all some kind of coordination of the village guards. Wasn't there anybody who was in charge of keeping a log, a roster of the people who were to take part in the guards, of the times and dates when these people were supposed to patrol? Wasn't there some kind of coordination?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Who would ask you to go on a patrol?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you made up the decision on your own? You decided to go on a specific night, to go for a round of two hours on the village guard; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We went, me and others, we heard that people were guarding the houses, so we did the same thing, and nobody assigned us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to articulate better what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you know Nenad Santic, Mr. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sure, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Were you in touch, did you have contacts, kind of a relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Who is Dragan Vidovic in relation to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He is my family, a relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did your cousin not have any responsibility in organising the village guards?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He did something, but it was with civil defence, the village civil defence, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Somehow he had responsibilities; he was in charge of organising the village guards?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Somebody perhaps was, I think, then, but that was the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm merely trying to understand how things were working at the time. You have to understand that. You are telling me that your cousin, Dragan Vidovic, because he was in the civil defence, had some kind of responsibility in organising the village guards? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. No. He wasn't responsible. I don't know how to put it. We elected him to see who wanted to, so that we could have some timetable to know who was going when.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, if I understood you well, you told us following the first conflict, that is, after the 20th of October, 1992, the village guards were done away with, were suppressed; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you absolutely certain of it, or are you simply saying that following the 20th of October, 1992, you no longer took part in the village guards?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (No discernible response)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not understand what the witness said. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your answer has not been understood, Mr. Vidovic. I am going to repeat the question. Are you absolutely sure that the village guards were abolished following the first conflict, or is it more simply so that you no longer took part in them, and that therefore you thought that they were no longer happening?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You do not rule out, however, that the village guards would have been going on, but with other people, with other volunteers? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Let us talk about the time when your family left for Germany in April '92. Your mother had been living for many years in Germany. Who made the decision?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My wife's mother was there. Her mother decided that. He called her from Germany and invited her to go there, so she went to Germany first in 1991 for a month or two to work, and then she invited her over, with children, because in Croatia there was war, it was beginning in Bosnia, and she told her to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Oh, I had understood that you were the one who had decided that your wife and your children had to go to Germany, but that wasn't so; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, you're right. This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why was that decision made by your mother-in-law, by your wife's mother?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: She invited her to go there to work a little, make some money, and that woman supported us, so we were obliged to her. "Cross through Croatia because later on you won't be able to." And so she went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So it is not actually because of the situation prevailing in Central Bosnia at the time, in April 1992, it is not for that reason that the decision was made by your mother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We received a summary of your testimony in which it is stated that in 1992, you sent your wife and children to Germany so as to make sure that they were safe, but it isn't true, is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that in September '92, you paid a visit to your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I returned after some 10 or 15 days because I went with a friend in his car, and that is how we went and came back. That was in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you first tell us why you didn't go with your family in April '92, why you didn't go with them to Germany?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was nobody else in the house, nobody else lived there, so I had to look after the house, and I had to go to work, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But couldn't you have found another job in Germany? This is nothing but a question, but I'm wondering. I don't have the answer for you, of course.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do what? When I don't know to do anything, I can't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore in September '92 you drove with a friend in a car to go and visit your wife and children in Germany. What's that friend's name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The friend is from Croatia. I don't really know. We went together, and we came back 10 or 15 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I forgot. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You forgot?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Whose car did you drive in?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His car. His privately owned car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And where did that friend live?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The friend lived in Vitez, and in Split for a longer period of time. In Split and in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Between Split and Vitez? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Vitez and Split. He was born in Split, but he lived in Vitez. So I went with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And you can't remember his name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His first name was Miso, but I can't remember his last name. Miso. I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where did you cross the border between Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Kamensko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And which route did you then follow from there on, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember this route. I don't know these roads very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How long was the journey, how many hours?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Two days, a day. Two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it one or two days? Is that one or two days?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, or a day and a half or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to give Exhibit D29/3 to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is this the passport from the former Yugoslavia which you had at the time of the journey?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that you behaved regularly, that you obtained a German visa in Salzburg, then crossed the border. On page 2 of the document, can you tell us which are the stamps related to the first journey?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see. I can't see. I can't see. Well, September. I got the visa in September, and the date, the date for entering Germany, I think it was mid-September. I think that it was in mid-September that I got the visa in Salzburg. The visa was valid until the 25th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you keep the original of that passport?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have the original here, it's at the hotel. It's an old one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us that you then returned to Bosnia and that you went back to Germany towards the end of March 1993. What did you have in mind? What were your intentions in terms of your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To go back home, naturally. To have my family return home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you were going to get your family. That's what you had in mind. That's what you wanted to do in order to bring your family back to Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, my wife and my two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We're now talking about the second journey, the journey of March 1993, according to your statement. You stated that before you left, you received an authorisation from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'll ask the usher to hand in to the witness Exhibit D28/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, on the top end of this document you see the permit issued by the HVO, upon your request, for a journey between the 22nd of March, 1993 and the 11th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Permit? Permit? I didn't understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat my question, Mr. Vidovic. You applied for a travel permit from the HVO for a period from the 22nd of March, 1993 until the 11th of April, 1993; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The two dates are written into the document signed by Marijan Skopljak, and this was on the basis of your indications, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I came to the municipality, and I asked for a permit to be given to me, and they gave me this. Yes. I submitted a request, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I understood that you applied for it, but my question is more specific. It relates to the dates in the document, because the trip is supposed to start on the 22nd of March, 1993 and end on the 11th of April, 1993. Are these the dates that are to be found in the document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are the dates. Yes. Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: These dates were written into the document after you had given some instructions or indications; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You were, therefore, planning to leave on the 22nd of March and to be returning on the 11th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was late. I arrived in Germany on the 1st of April, 1993, I arrived. That's why I stayed 10 or 15 days. I couldn't go back otherwise, because I didn't have documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How did you travel? Which means of transport did you have?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I travelled by bus. By bus. By bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where did you cross the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter didn't understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer? Where exactly did you cross the border between Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Kamensko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At the border did you show this document, the HVO document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But the authority you showed this document to didn't put any stamp on the paper?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have it. It's like a little card that shows that I crossed the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is that the card, a copy of which is to be found in the same document? Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The same, but the little card shows the date when I crossed the border, I mean, the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But no stamp was put on the HVO permit, because my question was more specific than that, on the HVO document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The Prosecutor is presenting incorrect data to the witness. He's saying, "So there is no stamp put by the authorities on this document," and I would like the question, therefore, to be reformulated because there is a stamp that was placed there by the authorities, so that it would be accurate, and we don't want the witness to be misled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I, of course, didn't plan to mislead the witness as is stated quite explicitly and quite clearly in the transcript. I referred my question to the HVO permit, to the document which is on the top of the page, but in another testimony a similar document was presented and introduced, and it had received the stamp at the crossing of the border. I was surprised that this document hadn't received such a stamp. This is only by way of explanation to Mr. Par. My question was a simple one --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry for interrupting. That is precisely my objection. There is a stamp here. The stamp is here where it says "Border crossing," and with your permission, I'm going to read what it says: "The Ministry of the Interior, Police, Split." It is here on the original, on the first page of this text. It was not translated, but it's an international text, so one can see that this is a border crossing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- the present. So we all have in mind the Exhibit D28/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation, Mr. Par. I thought these were the photocopies of two different documents. On the one hand there was the HVO permit, but in the lower half it was a border crossing card, and there, indeed, you can see a frame on the photocopy. But as a matter of fact, this is a photocopy of one and the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry if there was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Par. This is no longer a misunderstanding. I can move on forward to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, what were the conditions of your crossing the border to Germany on the 1st of April, 1993, as you said earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I crossed it illegally. I crossed the border without any documents, on this bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? What was the means of transport you were using to cross the border?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bus, bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The bus was not checked, was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, only two drivers and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So this bus with two drivers and yourself was not checked at all?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was checked, but I was sitting there with them, and they said, "We're going and you're coming with us," and that's how we crossed the border. This other driver was probably there at the checkpoint where they look at documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, but the representatives of the German policy who were at the border crossing, did they ask for your papers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You did not come across any member of the German police?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where exactly did you cross the border?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Salzburg.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you sure that you mean Salzburg?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you help me give him this third document, I think it's Exhibit D29/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In the meantime, can I ask a question, Mr. Terrier? I'd like to seek some clarification from Mr. Par. I too had the impression that this document, D28/3, on page 1, was made up of two different documents. It's not very clear, because on the one hand we have this permit dated the 16th of March, 1993, and on the other hand we have a document which is a document for entry into the Republic of Croatia, and there you have the date of the 22nd of March. So if I got it right, these are two different documents. You photocopied two different, isolated case on one in the same. Could we have the originals, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I shall obtain the original for the court, and I shall provide you with it. I haven't got a copy now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Terrier. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree with me if I said that this document which you have in front of you was issued to you so that you would have to leave Germany before the 6th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked for it because I said that I lost my old passport, and they gave me this, this permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Vidovic, I mean, a permit for what?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To get out of Germany. It's a document because I lost my passport. Then when I got this, I found my passport. So this is a document in order to leave Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you'd lost your passport, you applied for this document, and then you found your passport again?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As my wife was packing the bags she misplaced it somewhere, but then I thought that we had lost the passport. That's why I asked for this. But then, after a while, we found the old passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The German authorities, at least those that issued this document to you, did they ask you in which way you had entered the German territory?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did the authorities under which authorisation or power you were staying in Germany until March 1993 -- so you'd been staying there for about five months. Would you agree with me if I said that this is a type of document which is issued to aliens or foreigners which are illegally in the territory of a State, requiring such individuals to leave territory at the earliest convenience because they're not entitled, they're not authorised to sojourn in that territory?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I agree about the State, but then I couldn't enter Slovenia with this document. I found out from my brother. He said, "You can get out of Germany, but you can't get into Slovenia without a passport." The old Umag passport was no longer valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the question again. There must be some misunderstanding. I'm going to put it differently to you. Were you checked by the German police in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Who did you turn to to obtain such a document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But very explicitly, it obliges you to leave Germany prior to the 6th August, 1993. Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why did you apply for this document then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to get out and to get a passport in Croatia, because as a tourist over there I couldn't get a passport in Germany. So then I asked to go to my brother's to get a document made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why didn't you do so?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because my brother said, "You can't get into Slovenia. You can't cross the border with this piece of paper."

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, please refer back to Exhibit D29/3. Page 2. Page 2, on the right-hand page of your passport, a stamp can be seen which was affixed by the authorities or some authority of the German Republic. Could you tell us when that stamp was put in your passport and why it was affixed to your passport?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What don't you understand? Don't you understand the question, or the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The stamp that is on the right-hand page of your passport, and it is the second from the top. Can't you see a stamp saying "Bundesrepublik, Deutschland"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: My question was --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is for Zurich, that I was taken back from this border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, but as far as I know, Zurich is not in Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: He means "zuruck", meaning "return." You can see the other stamp. "Zuruck" means chased out of the country.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can't cross the border. You can't go back to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, my question was actually on the other stamp. I'm going to try my luck again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, on that page, there is indeed a stamp where you have the word Zuruckgewissen on it. But above that there is another stamp where you have "Bundesrepublik Deutschland." Can you see that one?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know this. I can see it, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Still, this stamp is to be found in your passport.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: However, you're not in a position to say when and why it was put there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to explain. When entry into the country is forbidden, then this stamp is put into the passport, Zuruckgewiessen and then this other stamp is affixed that is crossed out. So on the same occasion, I know that this is so, both of these stamps are affixed there, but the one that says "Bundesrepublik" is crossed out because the person did not enter the country. That I know personally. I know that it is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Par, could we have the original passport because the witness told us that he had that passport at the hotel. Could we have it tomorrow morning? I'm sure that it is possible to see the date in the passport, which is not to be deciphered here, because the photocopy is pretty poor. So, Mr. Par, can we have it by tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: By tomorrow morning I'll bring the original documents. So today we are not going to tender it into evidence until we have brought all of it in -- if the witness says that he does have it with him. So I'm going to inform you in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, he said already that he had the passport at the hotel. Yes, carry on, Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Another couple of questions and I will finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We're still talking about the same passport, the same page. There are two stamps we can see. A little bit to the left, one is December '92, and the other one is January '93. Could you tell us something about these stamps? What do they mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: '92, it was a visa allowing me to enter Germany, and it was issued for three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I don't think that is correct. I think the stamp which we have on the right-hand-side page of your passport, at the top of the page, you have a stamp. What does this stamp mean? No, this one, up here. The date, 10th of December, '92.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was when I went to Germany in December for Christmas. I went to visit my wife and my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I am rather confused, because we do not see here the date of your entry to Germany, but you now say you went for Christmas to Germany. Haven't you made any other trips? To Croatia, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to Croatia, and I also went to Germany. I did. I travelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, you travelled, that is why this stamp was put on your passport. So this was not a trip to Germany, it was a trip to Croatia; isn't that so? So according to your passport, you went to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I went to Germany. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So in December '92, you went to Germany?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Returning in January '93?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How many trips to Germany altogether?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Altogether, I went three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So, say, four times, according to your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, two or three questions more. First, according to these stamps that you've talked about, it does not seem that this stamp was placed by a German authority, but rather by a Croatian authority. Or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know either. I'm not sure either. They look at the passport. Whether they stamp it or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But in the document that you've showed us, there is absolutely no mention relative to the trip to Germany in March 1992. The only document, as we see, the photocopy, this is the crossing from Bosnia to Croatia in March '93, but we have nothing regarding Germany. Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The only German document that we have is this one, D29/3, that on the 22nd of July, '93, you are requested to leave Germany prior to 6 August because you are in Germany illegally. Or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're not right. I applied for the papers so as to leave Germany. That is the document. But not to enter another state with that document. I asked her for a paper to get out, but I could not enter Slovenia with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You said D29/3. Is it this document that you just quoted here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, it is D30/3. Yes, excuse me, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There is no point in discussing the debate, except we see that this is an expulsion order issued by Germany, and according to paragraph 42, paragraph 1 of the German law on aliens, and that is that particular document, yes, that we are talking about. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like D29/3 -- that is, a photocopy of his former Yugoslav -- be shown to the witness once again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you please take this photocopy and leaf through it, go through it from the first to the last page. Tell me how many pages this photocopy has.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please count them? Count them. How many?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What is on the first page?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the first page, the first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the page with your photograph. The catalogue is very short. And what about the second page?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The second page is the border crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, these photocopies which are attached as evidence to the Court record, are these the photocopies of your passport in its entirety, in toto? That is, was your passport photocopied in toto, in whole, or -- does your passport have more than two pages?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know how many pages there were in your passport?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But does it have more than two pages?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, sure it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So is this a photocopy of your whole passport, or a largish part of the passport was not photocopied?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is a part which wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So in practical terms, these are fragments of your passport?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you went to Germany for the first time, did you need a visa then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when was it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, between the former Yugoslavia and Germany visas were abolished, tourist visas. What I should like to know is, in 1992, when was it that you went to Germany first, for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when your family was in Germany already.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In September.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So in September 1992, when you went to Germany, did you need a visa then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, even if in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia there was one and the same passport, could one see from the passport which republic a person came from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Visa? No. Where the passport was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Next to the passport number, were there letters "BH"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What do these letters BH mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the initial letter in the passport from the former Socialist Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you know that there was only the letter "H"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said when you went to Germany for the first time, in 1992, that you were issued a German visa in Salzburg. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you then please describe this visa to us. Was it in the form of a stamp in your passport, or was it a kind of a card affixed to the passport like the Dutch visa now issued?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, it was a stamp in the passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So it was only a stamp in the passport?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And then it says from which date to what date that you could spend in the territory of the Federal Republic of Germany?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So as of September 1992 onwards, you needed a visa every time; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After these three months expired -- no, you mean within those three months you did not, but after these three months, then I needed a visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you need a visa again?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I needed it on the 22nd March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The last time you went there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had your passport at the hotel. We call it "putovnica" now. We used to call it "passport" then. Do you still have your former Yugoslav passport with you, or do you have your Croatian passport?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have a former Yugoslav passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You have the former Yugoslav passport? You brought it along?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that in that former Yugoslav passport there was the stamp which indicated the permit to enter Germany? Do you have an explanation, then, how is it possible that this document which was shown you by the Prosecution lacks this document? Is it because the whole passport was not photocopied?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you have the photocopy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: True, but this photocopy does not have it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But it's in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What is? The visa?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please show us in the Croatian text where that visa is supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: That is not the visa. There is a square stamp --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Right, but will you please bring the original of the passport tomorrow, so that we can see the rest of your passport which was not photocopied?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If you do not feel like coming here, you can send it either through us or through colleague Par, you can send your passport so we can see the original.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I see that my learned friend was surprised that you crossed from Austria into Germany on a bus without a passport and that nobody asked you about a passport.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked anything. We crossed the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what were the plates that the bus had?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. I never paid attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And those men, the driver and the co-driver, what language did you speak?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly Slovenian. They came from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So could we conclude that it was a Slovenian bus, then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably it was. I paid no attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you distinguish between Slovenian and Croatian languages?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do, some. They did say they were from Slovenia, they did travel, they worked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is whether you can distinguish between Slovenian and Croatian languages.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but poorly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you do not understand Slovenian well, but are you speaking Croatian or Slovenian?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: And would you notice a difference if I now spoke Slovenian?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Mirko, you had the original of this passport, the photocopy of which we showed today. Do you also have the originals of other documents that we showed here photocopied today? I'm referring to the permit and the paper from Frankfurt. Do you have them in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: You have both photocopies and the originals of both documents?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Tell us, please, this permit, what it says here, this is the border pass and the stamp that we talked about. Is it one document, or are these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These are two documents. They're both here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: The one below?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This card, if that is what you mean, it is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Will you please put it on the ELMO so that we can see it? And I do apologise, then. I do apologise to my learned friend and to Your Honours. I thought this was the stamp that you sealed the permit with, but the witness says that this is the card for the border crossing. Can we see it on the ELMO, please, the card. You have also the original of this permit, and you have the passport and this paper from the city of Frankfurt, and we promise to bring these documents tomorrow. Since I cut into my learned friend's examination because I thought that it was one and the same document, that now he has no right to cross-examine, if I may, I will ask now the question which I believe my learned friend had in mind at the time when I thought it was one and the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: So when you reached the border crossing with this pass, did the border authorities stamp that permit, or did they not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: When did they give you this pass, this one, that you just showed us?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I was crossing the border from Bosnia to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: On the Croatian side they gave you this?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They gave me this on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: I have no more questions, and tomorrow I shall present to the court the originals of the documents that the witness says he has with him, and tomorrow I shall tender it for itemisation. I have only one correction in the transcript, if I may. That is on page 111, twelfth line of the transcript, there was a mistake when the question was interpreted. My question to the witness, I asked him if he was in Germany from the 1st of April, 1993 until June '95, and the transcript says the 21st of April rather than the 1st of April. This is important, because we are seeking to prove that the witness was not in Ahmici on the 21st of April. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I have one question for the witness. Mr. Vidovic, are you a relative of Miro Vidovic in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, we are not related, not even distantly. There are several Mires. Don't know which one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I was referring to the one who died on the 18th of September, '93 in Pirici, according to the document Prosecution Exhibit 337.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We are not related, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Were there, either in Pirici, Santici, or Ahmici, other persons called Mirko Vidovic, having your name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: Another person called Mirko Vidovic, who has your name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is two or three more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You may now be released. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, we can't release you now because tomorrow you have to come back with your passport and the other documents, the original of the other documents which have been produced today by Defence Counsel Par. So you may now leave the courtroom, but please don't leave The Hague because, as I say, we may need you again. Thank you. We may move on to our next witness. In future, I think it would be appropriate for Defence counsel to always produce the original of any document they intend to put in in evidence. Yes. Let us now take a break, a 30-minute break. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovac, I presume. Good afternoon, Mr. Grabovac. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovac, would you introduce yourself to the court?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I'm Ivan Grabovac, born in Krcevine, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what year you were born in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I was born on the 15th of November, 1947.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where do you reside?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I reside in Krcevine, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the court where you were employed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: In 1992, I was employed in the Grill Restaurant that was owned by Ivica Kupreskic, and I had actually sublet it from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did you sublet this grill?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: On the 30th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what was this grill? Was it a restaurant or what?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: It was a restaurant of sorts. It offered grilled meat and a few things a la carte.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And where was this restaurant?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: This restaurant is in the centre of town, in the street of Kresimira Petra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, why did Mr. Ivica Kupreskic sublet this restaurant to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Because Ivica Kupreskic was supposed to go to Germany. I stayed on to work at The Grill as the owner of that shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say, not as the owner but as a person who was subletting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did you work there as the leasee of this restaurant?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I worked there until the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know why or, rather, whether Sutra, the company Sutra, had some shops of its own?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. It had a retail and a wholesale.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was the owner of the Sutra company?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Ivica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was the wholesale department of this enterprise and where was the retail store?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: The retail store was in town, in the building called Vucjak, and wholesale was in the village of Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the assortment of goods that this shop had? Was it food? Was it consumer goods?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: It offered mixed goods. There were food products there and, also, there were textiles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who worked in this retail store in the building in Vucjak in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Dragica Grabovac did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is Dragica Grabovac related to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, she's my sister.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Until when did she work at that store?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: She worked there until the 6th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did she work there as a saleslady?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, she worked as a salesperson, and she was in charge from a material and moral point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Why did she stop working there, in April 1993, in that shop?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: There were family problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What kind of problems?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Her oldest son's health, and then she had to leave the shop so that she could take care of her oldest son.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who came to replace her then at this shop in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Mirjan Kupreskic did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did Mirjan Kupreskic work until then; do you know?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: He worked at the wholesale in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is to say, in the same company but at a different place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, at a different place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The Grill Restaurant that you had sublet, did you get your supplies for it from this shop of Ivica Kupreskic in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I got supplies for that restaurant from the retail store of Sutra, all the products that were there in that shop. If there were some products that could not be obtained there, then I would purchase them elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So did you come to this shop in Vitez every day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No, not every day, only when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How often was that? How often per week, for example?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I'd come three days in a row, and sometimes I would the not come for an entire day and then I'd come on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Before the second conflict or, rather, before the war broke out in the Lasva River Valley, during that week, did you see Mirjan Kupreskic in that shop? Did you see him working there in the shop?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, every day, because in the morning we would have coffee together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, do you remember whether you were in the shop of Ivica Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to buy some goods. I went to get some Tuborg beer that you couldn't get in other stores, and I got all that they had left but not very much of it because there wasn't enough, not even at Mirjan's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You saw Mirjan working there, right, on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see Mirjan working there on that day, there at the shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you do then? Did you leave immediately or did you stay at the shop?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: On that day I came to the shop. I got the Tuborg beer. I put it into my own car. In the meantime, Krgovic Batric came and Mujcibabac Gavro too. I treated the two of them to a drink, while Mirjan Kupreskic asked me to go to the staircase by the office, because he didn't want his customers to see us drinking beer. I treated Krgovic Batric and Mujcibabic Gavro Mujcibabic, and we talked, just plain, everyday talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So where did you actually take a seat, was it in the warehouse or the storage area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was some kind of a storage area of that shop but not in the proper sense of the word, because people would pass there on their way to the office as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did anybody else come in after that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Veljko Cato came. He had finished his work, and he also offered us a drink or, rather, Tuborg beer that we were having that day. We talked there until about 4.00 p.m. Just before 4.00 p.m. we parted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And these two men who came at the beginning, this Krgovic Batric and Mujcibabic Gavro, are they your friends?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: They are pensioners. At that time, I was better off than pensioners. I wanted to treat them to a drink.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Well, we also had some meze. That's what you call these canapés with the drink.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You had a drink, didn't you? That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And why didn't Mirjan want to have people seen drinking at the shop?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Well, it's not right. It's not proper for customers who were coming in to shop to see us drinking beer. Children come there, women, and it's not proper for them to see us drinking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After that, what did you talk about as you were socialising there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: On that day, we talked about inflation the most, and Veljko Cato and I talked about this, saying that we could not keep up with inflation. Our prices could not keep up with inflation. We joked a bit, and we chatted, and this was everyday talk and the kind of jokes we always exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you talk about the abduction of Zivko Totic and the murder of his escorts and this political situation that was rather tense at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Not on that day, because we did not have a radio because we were sitting in front of the office, and we didn't know anything, not until I came home in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. When did you get home?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I came sometime between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who came to see you that evening? Who came to see you at your home -- that is to say, to your mother's house?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: My sister, Ankica Grabovac came, and her husband, Ivica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Ankica Grabovac is actually Ankica Kupreskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Ankica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: She's your sister; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did you see her?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: In the family house of my mother's and my sister-in-law -- or that is to say, my late brother's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: This is in Krcevine, number 90, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: She came to see her mother and to see her brothers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was Ankica Kupreskic before that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Ankica Kupreskic was in Germany for about a year and 15 days or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At what time did Ankica Kupreskic and her husband, Ivica, come in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: They came approximately around 7.00 p.m., ten past seven, quarter past seven; around 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: They stayed, I believe, about 30 minutes, until 7.30 or 7.40.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, all right. All of this is approximate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Ankica Kupreskic see all of her brothers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No. She saw me, Ivan, she saw Anto. Karlo, on that day, after work, he stayed in the cafe of Osman in Mahala in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That was a Muslim cafe, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the Muslim part of Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Karlo Grabovac was a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That evening he was not at home, but he was in a Muslim cafe; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On that evening did you receive any information that on the next day there would be a conflict between the Muslims and the Croats in the area of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No, because if my brother came after the curfew, I did not know of any stories about a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Had he known about this, had he had any information about a conflict, would he have informed you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Most probably he would have, but I cannot present his opinions now. I can't see this clearly in my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to ask you this at the end. So you have no information about the coming conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened in the morning in Krcevine?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: That night for me was like all the other nights before that. I watched television, and after some time I went to bed, and then in the morning we just heard shooting and shelling. That could have been around 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I don't think that the translation is right. Did you hear shooting, or shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I only heard shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where were the shells falling?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Partly they were falling on Vitez and partly on my village, called Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On which part of the village did these shells fall?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: The northern part and the central part of Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who lived in this central part of Krcevine?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did the shelling go on?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: The shelling went on for about half an hour, and then there would be a lull, and then again. That's the way it went that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there an army in the village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: At that moment there was not an army in the village. At our own initiative, we couldn't go through a wall. What is impossible is impossible. We gathered at around 5.00, and we gathered in the western part of the village, and we discussed all the troubles that had befallen us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At what time did you gather together the people from the village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Around 15.00 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Was there any shooting that day in the village? I mean, was there any small-arms fire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No. No. Only shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us how many Croats there were in that village?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
