utterances.text: According to the last census, of 1990, there were exactly 539 Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many rifles did you have in the village subsequently, when you met and then counted the rifles?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Around 15.00 that day, on the 16th, we met around 15.00 in the western part of the village, and we had 28 rifles. Of them, three were hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did the fighting break out, or rather when did the conflict with Muslims in Krcevine begin? When was that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: That day we were already deployed along the boundaries of the village. We did not know anything. There was no shooting for another day or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mean it began sometime on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, a little bit on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When were you mobilised, in fact?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I was mobilised to the boundaries of the village on the 17th of April, '93 -- or rather on the 18th of April '93. It was a Saturday -- no, it was Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When all was said and done, did you spend that war in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No. On Sunday, I finished at the boundaries of the village, and they moved to my personal car to transport wounded or dead. And that indeed happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, but after that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I did it until the 27th of July, '93. When we ran out of fuel, I was ordered back to the front line in my village, called Krcevine, from which I never went away until the cease-fire was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After the cease-fire was signed, where did you work? Did you stay with the HVO, or did you go into private business?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: As soon as we were allowed to turn in our weapons, I was among the first, and then Ivica Kupreskic took me on as a worker in his retail outlet to work as a salesman. I began to work in the beginning of May. It could have been the 3rd or the 4th of May when I was hired to work for Ivica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So it was a job that was Ivica Kupreskic's before the war, in the same shop?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At the same place?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: At the same place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Mirjan Kupreskic work at the time anywhere?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: At that time, Mirjan Kupreskic was already working at the wholesale store in Pirici. They opened their second store, wholesale store, at Vucjak, and Mirjan worked there as a wholesale dealer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So when you came on the 4th of May, '94, and began to work at that retail outlet, you found Mirjan Kupreskic, who was already working as a dealer, as a wholesale dealer, for the same company? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No. I took over the retail business from Mirjan, and Ivica opened that wholesale unit that Mirjan would then man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you succeeded him there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So on the 4th of May, he was already working. The important thing is that he began working before you; is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Mirjan Kupreskic work now for this wholesale unit in '94, '95, '96?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: He worked -- yes, for the wholesale unit in '94, '95, and '96.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You met him there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I stayed there such a short time, because I wanted to go back to my enterprise to work as a waiter, because I could also rent a facility, some premises, from my company, and I thought it would be easier to take some premises from the company than to look for one as a third person. Thus I went to Ivica Kupreskic, to his restaurant company, Kruscica, in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you happen to see Ivica Kupreskic in uniform before the war?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After the cease-fire was signed in April '94, did you ever see him wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No. Who wore that uniform during the war, that is, those who had it, they could not wait but get rid of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Will you tell me just one more thing: Those people who were in the store -- I'm talking about the 4th of May, '94 -- Krgovic Batric, Mujcibabic Gavro and Veljko Cato, do you know what their ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Mujcibabic Gavro and Veljko Cato are Orthodox; that is, Serbs. Krgovic Batric is a Montenegrin. I could not really tell you what his ethnic origin is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Montenegrin?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic, any cross-examination for any Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, other counsel for Defence have no intention -- are not planning to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovac, as a result of your testimony here today, I would like to ask you just a few questions arising from that. My name is Michael Blaxill, and I am one of the Prosecution attorneys assigned to this case. Sir, you said that on the 15th of April, 1993, you were having a beer at the store where Mirjan Kupreskic worked, and you used the expression that you parted at about 4.00. Does that mean that you personally left the shop at 4.00, about 4.00?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: That day I left the store around 16.00, perhaps a little before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you left the shop, where was Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Mirjan Kupreskic stayed behind in the store, in Ivica Kupreskic's shop, because the working hours were until 17.00, until 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic at all again on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No. After 16.00, I did not see Mirjan Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic at all during the subsequent days, the 16th, the 17th, or the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I saw Mirjan afterwards, whether it was seven, eight, or maybe ten days later. I came to the Grill Restaurant to throw away the meat which was in the refrigerator because all these items were perishable, and I took some beer home. That day I saw Mirjan Kupreskic in the town, only I cannot say which date it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. When you left on the 15th of April you left the shop, did you, in fact, go back to your Grill Restaurant at all, or did you go straight to your relatives' home?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No. I went to the Grill Restaurant, unloaded the beer, took it into the restaurant, and I was there for an hour, an hour and a half. Then I went directly home.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At what time, sir, do you recall arriving back home, if you do, indeed, recall?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I got home sometime before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe you said that you received a visit from your sister and her husband, Mr. Ivica Kupreskic, somewhere around 7.00 that evening; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No, they did not come to visit me. They came to see my mother at my late brother's, and I went over to their house to celebrate, to welcome my brother-in-law and my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you went to bed quite normally that night and slept through until about half past five the following morning. That would be correct, sir, yes?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: It is, except that I did not go to bed directly, because I usually stay up and watch TV and as there were all sorts of news, I wanted to hear them all, and that is what I did on that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then you've told us, sir, that you woke then in the morning and that the sounds that woke you were those of the sound of shelling, heavy gunfire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, because at that hour my body is already used to it. I sleep until about 7.00, but that morning the shelling woke me up around 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you go out of your house at that point or shortly after, or did you remain indoors because of the shelling that was going on?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: As soon as I heard the shelling, I dressed up and went out but without really knowing where to go and how to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You've given an opinion as to where the shells were falling in terms of Vitez and then some on your village. Could you actually see the fall or explosion of these shells, or was it the sound that led you to that belief?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Shells, these which fell, and the configuration of my village is such that you cannot see more than 20 per cent of it from one particular spot, but all the shells that came, came from the Zenica territory, that is, from Preocica, Lupac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How were you able to say that you knew they were coming from that direction? Again, was it the sound of shells travelling? What gave you that basis for that opinion?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Well, they could not come from any other side but the Zenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How far is your village of Krcevine -- I hope I'm pronouncing it correctly -- Krcevine from Ahmici? Can you say how far that is, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Krcevine is about -- somewhere around eight to nine kilometres away from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that any events that occurred in Ahmici between, indeed, say, the 16th of April onwards through that month, you would have no knowledge of those events directly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Something was known but it was all rumours. There were no reliable sources to learn from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It seems from within your community there was no shooting, small-arms shooting, between people for perhaps another day or two after the 16th; is that right? I think you said that it was the 18th that that started.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: At that point, I think you've used the expression of being mobilised, but had you had any village, or community, or civilian defence duties that he had performed or that you were enlisted to perform in the event of such a conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: No, we did not have any duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you in any way a member of the HVO prior to the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: I was only a member of the HDZ, not the HVO, because at that time, I was already a man of advanced age, a man of 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was the manner in which you were mobilised on the 18th of April? How did you receive the information that you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: That day, I'm going back to the 17th when we met at our own initiative, the President of the neighbourhood community of Krcevine, Ivan Zuljevic said, "This doesn't all go well," and, "We've got to get to the boundaries of the village." I stayed there until Sunday, when that selfsame Ivan Zuljevic told me that I should instead take my own car in order to transport the wounded and the dead, and that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Grabovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That is the conclusion of my cross-examination, Your Hounours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Grabovac, will you tell us how many members of your family were killed in this war, just to see how many?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: In my family, blood relatives, 18 persons were killed, including those three times removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you said the shelling came from Preocica, Lupac, Zenica, or Preocica and Lupac, ethnically speaking, what villages are those, Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Preocica is mostly a Muslim village with several orthodox or, rather, Serb families.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And Lupac?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Lupac was a purely Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that shelling came from the direction of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Not from Zenica but from the direction of Zenica, because Preocica and Lupac were at a much higher altitude than my village. My village is several hundred metres below these two villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I just want to ask you to tell us -- I don't know if you understood my learned friend from the Prosecution properly. He asked you if you had any duties in the village, whether there were any village guards, among other things. Were there village guards in Krcevine?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but we did not carry any weapons for anything but just because of crime. In my village, there were about 25 or 26 Muslim families, and they also carried rifles in order to protect their families because of crime. On various occasions, this so-called ramp, that is where the railway tracks passed, that is where we met with Muslims who had rifles. That is one or two rifles, just as we did, one or two when we were on duty. We would greet one another as neighbours, as brothers, not -- unaware what was in store for us in the days to come.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you are saying that you carried a rifle because of crime, you mean that you did not carry it to defend yourselves against Muslims; is that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRABOVAC
utterances.text: It is, because crime appeared, and in the village it happened often that somebody could not come and so there was the empty space. There was nobody to look after the village, to patrol the village, and we simply visited several houses where I lived in the western part and also in the other part, in the northern part from Preocica, and they did the same thing. But it did happen, for instance, that nobody would be anywhere around the place and yet we feared criminals and we wanted to protect our village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Grabovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions. Thank you so much, Mr. Grabovac, for testifying. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We could probably call the next witness, Mr. Safradin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, unfortunately, we didn't manage to get another witness for today. That would have been the fifth witness, and we thought that -- well, we have some certain problems with the witnesses, so we're going to have our next witness tomorrow. This decision to change the schedule, that you took, also resulted in the fact that we did not have enough witnesses in The Hague, because instead of working Wednesday all day, we were notified that we would spend all day Monday here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We do appreciate that. Thank you. So we will start tomorrow with Mr. Safradin, but we have noticed that out of the what, seven remaining witnesses, four are character witnesses. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Only two will be character witnesses, and two are going to give some information on facts related to the events of the 15th and/or 16th, and these facts are already contained in the summary, in the summary of their statements. That is to say, they are not going to be testifying about new facts but only those that are mentioned there. There are only two character witnesses that we'd like to hear. As for the rest, we are going to give signed statements, signed and certified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you may remember that we, on the 17th of February, '99, issued an order which, among other things, requested Defence counsel to refrain from asking fact witnesses questions which are designed solely to prove the good character of the accused and, more generally, we called upon Defence counsel to refrain from calling character witnesses. I, of course, will admit these two character witnesses, but we would like to suggest that the Defence counsel should confine themselves to a very brief examination-in-chief. In particular, you don't need, I think, to go into this question of the folklore club because, I think, this has not been disputed by the Prosecutor and, I think, we heard a lot of evidence about that particular club, and dancing, and so on. All right. So we will adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00. Tomorrow we will be sitting from 9.00 until 1.30. No sitting in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: at 5.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of March, 1999 at 9.00 a.m.
